mishnayot.title: Two people grip a cloak
mishnayot.summary: When two people each claim a cloak and neither can prove it, each swears and they divide it by what each claims.

b: Two people are grasping a cloak, each saying "I found it" or "it's all mine," and neither can prove it. With no witnesses, the judges rely on an oath.
Kulp 1:1
Oaths were taken very seriously, so an oath is a strong deterrent to lying.
Kulp 1:1
Each swears that he owns no less than half of the cloak, and they split it.
Mishnah 1:1

outline.h: One claims all, the other claims half
b: The one who says "it's all mine" swears that he owns no less than three quarters; the one who says "half is mine" swears that he owns no less than a quarter.
Mishnah 1:1
The first takes three quarters and the second takes a quarter.
Mishnah 1:1

chart.title: How the cloak is divided
rows: One says all, the other says half

picture: Both claim all of it: they swear, and divide it in half.
picture2: One claims all, the other half: three quarters and a quarter.

mishnayot.title: Two men and a donkey
mishnayot.summary: Two men on one animal each say it is all theirs: they swear and split its value. If they agree or there are witnesses, no oath is needed.

b: Two men were riding on an animal, or one was riding and the other leading it. Each says it is all his.
Mishnah 1:2
Each swears that he owns no less than half, and they split it.
Mishnah 1:2
If after the case is settled they both admit the other's claim, or there are witnesses, they split the animal without an oath.
Mishnah 1:2
The oath only ensures the person is telling the truth; when nobody disputes it, or witnesses testify, there is no need, and it is better to avoid oaths.
Kulp 1:2

chart.title: Splitting the animal
rows: They later admit each other's claim, or there are witnesses

picture: Two men, one donkey, both claiming it. Left: they swear. Right: they agree, with a witness, and no oath is needed. Either way they split it half and half.

mishnayot.title: Lost property seen from a donkey
mishnayot.summary: A claim of ownership has to come when you hold the object, not after you have already given it away.

b: A man was riding on a beast and saw lost property and said to his friend, "Give it to me." The friend picked it up and said "I have acquired it": he has acquired it.
Mishnah 1:3
But if he first handed it to the rider and only then said "I acquired it first," he has said nothing.
Mishnah 1:3
The claim to ownership must come at the same time that he actually has possession, not after he has already given it to someone else.
Kulp 1:3

chart.title: Who keeps the lost object?
rows: Picks it up and says "I acquired it"
Gives it to the rider, then says "I had it first"

picture: He picked it up and said he acquired it: it is his.
picture2: He handed it to the rider and only then claimed it: his claim means nothing.

mishnayot.title: Seizing lost property, and the field that acquires
mishnayot.summary: Someone who falls on a lost object loses it to whoever seizes it first. A field can acquire an animal that cannot leave it.

b: If a man saw lost property and fell upon it, and someone else came and seized it, the one who seized it acquired it.
Mishnah 1:4
He saw people running in his field after lost property, such as a deer with a broken leg or pigeons that cannot fly, and said "my field acquires it": he has acquired it.
Mishnah 1:4
But if the deer was running normally or the pigeons flying, and he said it, he has said nothing.
Mishnah 1:4
Others have not yet claimed it, the animal is physically unable to leave the field, and the owner of the field claims it.
Kulp 1:4

chart.title: Does the field acquire it?
rows: Deer with a broken leg, or pigeons that cannot fly
A deer running normally, or pigeons flying

_pending_picture: A deer with a broken leg cannot leave the field: "my field acquires it" works.
_pending_picture2: A healthy deer can run off, and the pigeons fly: it doesn't.

mishnayot.title: Who owns what a family member finds?
mishnayot.summary: What those who are supported by him find belongs to him; what those who are independent of him find is their own.

b: What is found by his minor son or daughter, his Canaanite slave or female slave, or his wife.
Mishnah 1:5

A father who supports his children can claim what they earn, including found objects; a Canaanite slave is wholly owned and cannot own property; a wife supported by her husband gives him her earnings.
Kulp 1:5
What is found by his grown son or daughter, his Hebrew slave or female slave, or his divorced wife, even if he has not yet paid her ketubah.
Mishnah 1:5
A father's control does not extend to adult children he does not support; a Hebrew slave is like a hired worker; a divorced woman owes him no earnings.
Kulp 1:5

picture: A small child's find goes to the father: he keeps it.
picture2: A grown daughter's find is her own: she keeps it.

mishnayot.title: Found debt documents
mishnayot.summary: Whether to return a found loan document depends on whether it records a lien on the debtor's property.

outline.h: A lien on the debtor's property
b: He should not return it, since the court would collect repayment from the property.
Mishnah 1:6
Rabbi Meir: he may return it, since the court would not collect from the property.
Mishnah 1:6
The Sages: in either case he should not return it, since in either case the court would collect from the property.
Mishnah 1:6

mishnayot.title: Found documents of giving
mishnayot.summary: Documents that give something to another person are not returned, since the writer may have changed his mind.

b: A man who found bills of divorce, writs of emancipation, wills, deeds of gift or receipts should not return them.
Mishnah 1:7
The writer may have written one and then changed his mind and decided not to give it.
Mishnah 1:7
These documents are normally kept by the recipient, so one might expect to return them to him, but we cannot be sure the recipient lost it.
Kulp 1:7

picture: A found document of this kind is not returned: perhaps it was lost after it was given (left), or the writer changed his mind and never gave it (right).

mishnayot.title: Documents that are returned, and the one that waits for Elijah
mishnayot.summary: Which found documents are returned, and what to do with one of unknown nature.

b: Letters of evaluation or sustenance, documents of halitzah or refusal, documents of arbitration, and any document drawn up by the court.
Mishnah 1:8
Documents found in a satchel or bag, or a bundle of documents (three tied together).
Mishnah 1:8
If it is an identifiable bag, return them to the person who can identify it.
Kulp 1:8
Three documents in which one man borrowed from three others: return them to the borrower.
Mishnah 1:8
Three documents in which one man lent to three: return them to the lender.
Mishnah 1:8
A set of three documents with the same name was probably lost by that named person.
Kulp 1:8
A document of unknown nature found among his own documents is left until Elijah comes: he may neither discard it nor give it to creditor or debtor.
Mishnah 1:8 and Kulp 1:8
If there are postscripts with them, he does what the postscript says, even if the document is torn or unreadable.
Mishnah 1:8 and Kulp 1:8
